title: Enterprise Avalanche Surge: Preparation and Stabilization Playbook
author: Marcus Lee
body:
Summary:
This playbook describes the end-to-end procedures for preparing for, detecting, and stabilizing a sudden high-volume traffic event we call an "avalanche surge" for enterprise tenants (e.g., large customer marketing campaigns, viral product hooks, or third-party spikes). It covers pre-cutover preparation, detection thresholds, immediate actions (first 15–60 minutes), escalation behavior, automated mitigations, safe-failback, customer communications templates, and post-incident QBR artifacts.

When to use this playbook:
- Any customer-facing production spike where observed request volume, token throughput, or request concurrency increases by >= 5x baseline within a 5 minute window.
- Alerts triggered by the Avalanche Detector rule (see Telemetry) or when a customer reports widespread latency / 5xxs tied to a single tenant.

Goals and acceptance criteria:
- Preserve customer-visible availability (success rate >= 99.5%) during surge where possible.
- Maintain 95th percentile token latency <= 2x baseline SLO for dedicated tenants; notify if this cannot be met.
- Ensure cost containment and fairness across multi-tenant pools (automatic throttles engaged when thresholds are hit).
- Provide clear, timely communications to stakeholders and customers within 15 minutes of detection.

Key services and components referenced:
- ingress-proxy (tenant routing / ingress rate shaping)
- model-router (routes to model variants: full, quantized, low-cost-fallback)
- kvcache (KV cache for prefix reuse)
- rate-limiter (per-tenant quotas and adaptive throttling)
- telemetry-gatekeeper (synthetic checks, avalanche detector)
- batch-gateway (batched inference for asynchronous workloads)
- billing-telemetry (cost-attribution and anomaly flags)

Pre-runbook: preparation checklist (owner: customer-success + eng-sre)
1) Tenant profiling: ensure each enterprise customer has a current surge profile in the tenant registry. Profile fields: typical QPS, peak QPS observed historically, critical endpoints, consumer-facing SLAs.
2) Canary thresholds: add tenant to synthetic canary with 30s and 10s latency checks; ensure synthetic runner frequency is 1m during high-risk windows.
3) Capacity reservations: for Dedicated customers verify reserved GPU capacity is provisioned and autoscale policy is set (min, target, max).
4) Communication plan: assign primary CSM, escalation engineer (oncall SRE), and product contact. Document these contacts on the tenant row in the Customer Ops spreadsheet.
5) Automated fallback policy: ensure the tenant has an allowed fallback model-variant list and an explicit fallback policy (e.g., prefer quantized-7b then low-cost-llama if full model unavailable).
6) Cost protections: optional quota-protector enabled for tenant with threshold 2x baseline QPS by default.

Telemetry and detection (owner: eng-sre / telemetry):
- Avalanche Detector rule: 
  - Trigger when tenant QPS >= 5x baseline over 5 consecutive minutes OR 95th-token-latency >= 3x baseline for 6+ minutes.
  - Secondary triggers: sudden KV cache miss ratio > 50%, rate-limiter saturation, or sustained 5xx > 0.5% for 10 minutes.
- Dashboards to monitor: Tenant Surge Overview, Pool Utilization, Model Router Latency by variant, Rate-limiter saturation heatmap, KVC cache hit/miss.
- Automatic Pager: if Avalanche Detector triggers, send page to SRE oncall with priority P1 and notify CSM and account owner via email/SMS bridge.

Immediate response (first 0–15 minutes):
1) Triage owner acknowledges alert within 2 minutes.
2) Run a quick impact sweep: check error rates, 95th latency, queue depth on ingress-proxy, and which model-variant is receiving traffic.
3) Communication out: send initial customer-facing note (template below) within 15 minutes.
4) If available capacity exists in dedicated pool: issue temporary horizontal scale:
   - CLI: rcap scale --tenant <TENANT_ID> --pool dedicated --delta +2 --reason "avalanche temporary"
5) If autoscale cannot provision fast enough, initiate controlled throttling:
   - Increase per-tenant rate-limiter token cost for non-critical routes by 50% (see routing rule list).
   - Enable adaptive batching for synchronous endpoints where latency impact is acceptable.
6) Activate model-router fallback: shift a percentage of traffic to lower-cost quantized variants. Example policy: 30% -> 60% -> 100% over 10-minute windows if success rate stabilizes.

Stabilization checklist (minutes 15–60):
- Observe error rate and latency trends every 60s.
- If 5xxs remain high after fallback and throttles, escalate to multi-tier mitigations:
  - Enable per-endpoint backpressure headers to clients (Retry-After).
  - Move non-critical tenants on same pool to spillover routing.
  - Offload heavy batch workloads to batch-gateway with relaxed latency SLA.
- If costs are rising quickly, flip on the quota-protector to enforce hard cap; notify customer immediately.

Escalation and ownership matrix:
- CSM: primary customer comms, coordinates commercial/cost decisions.
- SRE oncall: technical triage and execution of scaling/route changes.
- Serving runtime lead (if >30 minutes): coordinates kernel/quantization swap or emergency model-reload.
- Product PM (optional): decides on temporary feature gating if surge is caused by a new product hook.

Automated mitigations (what we rely on):
- Adaptive batching toggle (runtime flag): toggles between low-latency and high-throughput batch profiles.
- KV cache aggressive TTL fallback: short-circuit cache rehydration for high churning prefixes.
- Prefill cold KV for high-frequency prefixes using synthetic runner.
- Traffic-splitting policy: automated progressive traffic shifting to fallback variants with health checks.

Safety and rollback (safe-failback):
1) If degradation persists or customer explicitly requests rollback, revert traffic split to primary model and drain fallback nodes gracefully.
   - CLI: model-router set-split --tenant <TENANT_ID> --primary 100 --fallback 0 --drain 300s
2) If scaling caused noisy neighbor effects, revert temporary scale and open a capacity incident to procure additional GPUs.
3) Record all changes with runbook tags and timestamps. Use audit CLI: runbook log --incident <INC_ID> --changes "..."

Customer communications (templates):
- Initial (within 15m):
  Subject: [Redwood] We detected elevated traffic for your account — initial update
  Body: Hello <CustomerName>,

  We detected a sudden increase in traffic for your account beginning at <time>. Our automated systems flagged an "avalanche" event and our operations team is actively stabilizing traffic. Expected impacts: transient increased latency and limited throttling on non-critical routes. We will follow up in 15 minutes with more detail.

  Owner: <CSM name> | support@redwood.ai | Escalation: +1-555-0123

- Follow-up (30–60m):
  Subject: [Redwood] Update on traffic surge for your account — actions taken
  Body: Hello <CustomerName>,

  Summary of actions taken: enabled adaptive batching, progressive model fallback (quantized variants), and temporary rate shaping on non-critical endpoints. Current status: success rate: 99.3% (target 99.5%), 95th-token-latency: 1.8x baseline. Next steps: monitoring and preparing safe-failback.

  If you need to pause traffic from your side we recommend returning HTTP 429 with Retry-After.

Post-incident actions and QBR artifacts (owner: CSM + SRE):
- Incident timeline with all runbook logs and CLI commands.
- Cost delta report: compute minutes used vs baseline and estimated bill impact.
- Root-cause hypothesis and mitigation grooming ticket for product/serving teams.
- Customer-facing RCA draft and final RCA with timeline and preventative actions.
- Add a segment to the next QBR titled "Surge events and capacity readiness" including:
  - What happened, customer impact, timeline of mitigations, residual risk, recommended capacity reservations, and any commercial remedies.

Operational playbook snippets (CLI examples):
- Scale dedicated pool: rcap scale --tenant TEN-42 --pool dedicated --delta 3 --tag "avalanche-temp"
- Set progressive fallback: model-router split --tenant TEN-42 --primary 70 --fallback 30 --policy progressive-10m
- Lock quota-protector: quota-protector lock --tenant TEN-42 --limit 2x-baseline --reason "avalanche"

Postmortem checklist (owner: SRE lead):
1) Collect telemetry (raw traces, ingress logs, model router metrics, KV cache traces).
2) Annotate timeline with all automated interventions and human actions.
3) Complete RCA within 7 business days and share with customer and internal stakeholders.
4) Propose concrete changes: autoscale tweak, pre-warming policy, fallback variants list update, cost-guard thresholds.

Appendices:
A. Quick triage matrix (one-page):
- Symptom: High 95th latency; Likely cause: KV cache miss spike or model hot path saturation; Immediate action: enable quantized fallback, prefill KV, scale.
- Symptom: Rising 5xx; Likely cause: ingress-proxy queue overflow; Immediate action: enable backpressure headers, spill to batch gateway, scale ingress.

B. Dashboard IDs and links: Tenant Surge Overview: dash-ops-tn-surge-17; Model Router Health: dash-model-router-04; KV Cache Monitor: dash-kvcache-02.

C. Recommended QBR slides (bullets):
- Event summary, mitigation timeline, compute delta, recommended SLA/commit changes, open action items with owners and target dates.

Document ownership and review cadence:
- Owner: Customer Success (playbook steward)
- Technical reviewer: Eng SRE (runtime stability)
- Review cadence: annual or after any enterprise-scale surge incident.

Revision history:
- 2026-11-10: Initial draft (Marcus Lee).
